speaker_role: student panel (current Princeton undergraduates, one of whom also runs a paid consulting channel) -- not admissions officers
commercial_incentive: video is sponsored by Bullseye Admissions, a paid college consulting/test-prep company, with an on-screen discount code and endorsement; the host himself is a paid private admissions consultant
key_insights: International applicants reportedly face tougher relative competition for a smaller pool of seats at highly selective US schools, though panelists say schools are actively trying to grow international enrollment.
Not offering AP courses at a student's home school is not necessarily disqualifying; both panelists say they were admitted to Princeton without ever taking an AP class.
English proficiency reportedly matters more for humanities-track applicants than STEM-track applicants, where subject-matter mastery is weighted more heavily than language polish.

Because formal recommendation letters are unfamiliar in some countries, students should seek teachers (ideally an English teacher, who may write more fluently) who know them personally rather than defaulting to the most prestigious or subject-relevant teacher.

Some private US universities offer their own financial aid application for international students that bypasses fee-based intermediary systems, but aid must be reapplied for every year, not just as an incoming freshman.

International students lacking access to labs or extracurricular infrastructure can self-initiate projects (e.g., ordering hobby electronics kits, cold-emailing professors) to demonstrate initiative, which the panelists say colleges value.

One panelist advises choosing activities from genuine interest rather than purely for application value, arguing authentic effort is both more distinctive and more personally rewarding regardless of admissions outcome.
specific_numbers_or_facts: About 10% of Princeton's student body is international, per panelist Monica
Roughly three letters of recommendation per university are typical for international applicants, per panelist Ananya
notable_or_distinctive: Offers a firsthand international-student perspective on navigating unfamiliar systems, such as US-style recommendation letters and financial aid forms, rather than a US-based advisor's secondhand description of the same issues.
reliability_notes: Speakers are undergraduates giving personal, anecdotal impressions rather than admissions officers, so claims about competitiveness or admissions-officer opinions are unverified secondhand impressions (one is explicitly attributed to 'one of my interviewers'); the video contains an embedded paid sponsorship for a consulting company the host promotes without disclosed independent vetting.
